# Leaky buckets, gently

Rate limiting protects a service from being overwhelmed by too many requests in a short window. Instead of failing unpredictably under load, a rate-limited service rejects or delays excess requests in a controlled way, and tells the client when it may try again. A leaky bucket smooths traffic instead of tolerating bursts: requests enter a queue that drains at a constant rate, and requests arriving when the queue is full are dropped. It produces a very even output rate at the cost of added latency for bursty clients. The token bucket algorithm keeps a counter of available tokens that refills at a fixed rate up to a maximum capacity. Each request consumes one token; when the bucket is empty the request is rejected. Because tokens accumulate while the service is idle, the bucket tolerates short bursts without exceeding the long-term average rate. Choosing an algorithm is mostly a question of what you want to protect: a database that degrades under bursts prefers a leaky bucket, an API that sells quota to customers prefers a token bucket, and a shared cache with limited memory prefers sliding windows.
